Where it began

Steve Waugh was born in Sydney on 2 June 1965, four minutes ahead of his twin brother Mark, and the two grew up in the south-western suburb of Panania in a family that loved its sport. Their first game of cricket was not a triumph: both were out for nought. They recovered. As boys they were as good at soccer as at cricket, and in 1976 they became the youngest players ever picked for the New South Wales primary schools soccer side, which Steve later captained.

Cricket won in the end. The twins played first grade for Bankstown at 17, and Steve first played for the state side in 1984–85, scoring 71 alongside the tail in that season's Sheffield Shield final as his side won it.

The player

He began as a bowling all-rounder with a clever slower ball, and his calm in the final overs of the 1987 World Cup, which Australia won, earned him the nickname Iceman. Back trouble later made him a batter first, and what a batter. He played 168 Tests between 1985 and 2004, more than anyone before him, and made 10,927 runs at 51.06 with 32 hundreds, as well as taking 92 wickets.

The great innings came in clusters. In the 1989 Ashes he made 177 not out at Leeds and 152 not out at Lord's, and was not dismissed until he had 393 runs. In Jamaica in 1995 he batted for nine hours for 200 as Australia won the Frank Worrell Trophy, and at Old Trafford in 1997 he made a hundred in each innings. As captain from 1999 to 2004 he led Australia in 57 Tests and won 41, and he lifted the 1999 World Cup as one-day captain.

What made him special

Determination. As a young man he was a free, attacking strokemaker; in his prime he was the batter who would stay out there for as long as his team needed, and he had a knack of getting the best out of the tail. He was famously hard to intimidate.

His early Test years were patchy, and his first hundred did not arrive until his twenty-seventh Test. He clearly enjoyed it, because he went on to make 32 in all.

Away from the middle

Batting with his twin was a lifelong theme. In 1990 the brothers put on an unbroken 464 for New South Wales against Western Australia, a world first-class record, and in 1991 at Trinidad they were the first twins ever to share a Test team. Their younger brother Dean also played first-class cricket.

His charity work made him Australian of the Year in 2004, and was honoured with the Order of Australia, the Australian Sports Medal and a place among the National Trust's Australian Living Treasures. When he played his last Test, at Sydney, his team-mates carried him on a lap of honour.

And finally

After that 200 in Jamaica sealed the series in 1995, he went to bed in his whites, his socks and his baggy green cap. Some days are too good to take your kit off.
